ski.e: From Norwegian ski, from Old Norse skíð (“stick of wood, snowshoe”), from Proto-Germanic *skīdą (“stick”), from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to cut, split”) (see also shed).
ski.g: One of a pair of long flat runners designed for gliding over snow or water.

skilfulness.g: The state or condition of being skilful.

skill.e: From Middle English skill, skille (also schil, schile), from Old Norse skil (“a distinction, discernment, knowledge”), from Proto-Germanic *skilją (“separation, limit”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to split, cut”).
skill.g: A capacity to do something well; a technique, an ability, usually acquired or learned, as opposed to abilities that are regarded as innate.

skill.e: From Middle English skilen (also schillen), partly from Old English scilian (“to separate, part, divide off”); and partly from Old Norse skilja (“to divide, separate”); both from Proto-Germanic *skilōną, *skiljaną (“to divide, limit”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to split, cut”).

skillful.e: From Middle English skilful, skylfull, scelvol, equivalent to skill + -ful.

skillfully.e: From Middle English skilfully, skylfully, skilfulliche, equivalent to skillful + -ly.
skillfully.g: In a skillful manner; with skill.

skim.e: From Middle English skemen, skymen, variants of scumen, from Old French escumer (“to remove scum”), from escume (“froth, foam”), from Frankish *skūm (“froth, foam”), from Proto-Germanic *skūmaz (“foam”), from Proto-Indo-European *skew- (“to cover, conceal”).
skim.g: To pass lightly; to glide along in an even, smooth course; to glide along near the surface.

skin.e: From Middle English skyn, skinn, from Old English scinn, from Old Norse skinn (“animal hide”), from Proto-Germanic *skinþą, from Proto-Indo-European *sken- (“to split off”), nasal variant of *skeh₁i-d- (“to cut”). Partially displaced native Old English hȳd (“skin, hide”), from which derives hide.
skin.g: The outer protective layer of the body of any animal, including of a human.

skink.e: Possibly from Middle Low German schink, schinke, schenke (“leg; shank; shin bone; ham”), from Old Saxon skinka, from Proto-West Germanic *skinkō (“shank; thigh; that which is bent”), from Proto-Germanic *skinkô, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keng- (“to limp; to be crooked, slant”).
From Middle English skinken, skynken, skenken, from Middle Dutch scinken, scenken, schenken and/or Old Norse skenkja, both from Proto-Germanic *skankijaną.

skinned.e: From skin (“to remove skin”, verb) + -ed (suffix forming past tenses).
skinned.g: Having skin (or similar outer layer) totally or partially removed.

skip.e: From Middle English skippen, skyppen, of North Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skupjaną, perhaps related to *skeubaną (“to drive, push”), iterative *skuppōną (“to push/move repeatedly, skip”), from Proto-Indo-European *skewbʰ- (“to push, throw, shake”).
skip.g: To move by hopping on alternate feet.

skip.e: From Middle English skep, skeppe, from Old English sceppe, from Old Norse skeppa, skjappa (“basket, bushel, measure”), perhaps from Middle Low German scheppe (“a unit of weight”), perhaps related to Middle Low German schēpel (“buschel, measurement for grain”), German Scheffel (“bushel”). These could all ultimately be related to *skap (“shape”).
skip.g: A large container for waste, designed to be lifted onto the back of a truck to remove it along with its contents, or to be picked up by hydr

skirt.e: From Middle English scyrt, skirt, skyrte, skyrthe, skyrtte, from Old Norse skyrta, from Proto-Germanic *skurtijǭ (“apron; skirt”), from *skurtaz (“short; deficient”), from *skertaną (“to cut off”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut off; to divide”).
skirt.g: A separate article of clothing, usually worn by women and girls, that hangs from the waist and covers the lower torso and part of the legs.

skull.e: From Middle English sculle, scolle (also schulle, scholle), probably from a dialectal form of Old Norse skalli (“bald head, skull”), itself probably related to Old English sċealu (“husk”), to Proto-Norse *ᛋᚲᚨᛚᛟ (*skalo), from Proto-Germanic *skallô; compare Finnish kallo. Possibly related to Latin celsus (“lofty, high, tall”), collis (“hill”).
skull.g: The main bones of the head considered as a unit; including the cranium, facial bones, and mandible.

sky.e: Partly displaced Old English heofon, which survives in the reflex heaven, still sometimes used in the sense of sky, but usually in high or poetic register. It is also related to Old English scūa (“shadow, darkness”), Latin obscūrus (“dark, shadowy”), Sanskrit स्कुनाति (skunāti, “he covers”).
sky.g: The atmosphere above a given point, especially as visible from the surface of the Earth as the place where the sun, moon, stars, and clouds

sky.e: From Volsci (“a tribe who opposed the Romans”).
